questions_asked: How far would an Asian giant hornet queen typically fly from her nest when looking for a spot to start a new colony the following spring?
In your experience reviewing these hornet reports, which reports are most often wasted trips, with no hornet actually found?
In Washington State, how much field effort does one hornet report investigation usually take in person-hours?
How long would a Washington state agency typically wait before following up on a new hornet report?
When did the last confirmed Asian giant hornet sighting in the Pacific Northwest turn out to be a dead end?
How many staff can the Washington state hornet response team assign to report follow-ups at one time?
How many new hornet reports does the state typically receive in a busy late-summer week?
In what month do most Asian giant hornet reports in Washington State usually come in?
What would make a state entomologist confident an Asian giant hornet is really gone from an area?
When new hornet reports keep arriving in an area, do teams usually investigate them first or the older ones first?
expert_answers: About 30 km. That is the figure given in the problem statement as the estimated range for a new queen establishing her nest, and it matches the order of magnitude commonly cited for *Vespa mandarinia* dispersal (roughly 20–40 km, with most new nests founded much closer to the parent nest).

The wasted trips are overwhelmingly the ones with no usable evidence attached: reports with no photo, or a photo that is blurry, distant, or shows only a flying insect, plus reports whose Notes describe something generic ("big bee," "large wasp," "hornet in my yard") with no size, color, or location detail. Sightings far from the known detection area, and those submitted long after the stated detection date, also tend to come back negative. In practice the confirmed positives cluster in reports with a clear close-up image and notes mentioning a large orange-and-black head or the distinctive massive size.

Typically a few person-hours per report, not a full day. A standard follow-up is one or two staff driving to the site, spending roughly 30–60 minutes on site looking for the insect or nest, plus travel time — so on the order of 2–4 person-hours for a nearby report, and more (up to a full day) if the site is remote or requires a trap check and nest search. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.

Typically within a few days to about two weeks of the report being submitted. Reports with a clear photo or notes suggesting a genuine *Vespa mandarinia* (large orange-and-black head, unusually large size) are prioritized and followed up within a day or two, especially during the late-summer/fall detection season. Lower-priority reports — no photo, vague description, or a location far from the known detection area — may sit for weeks or never be investigated at all given limited resources. This is an empirical judgment based on typical agency practice, not a fixed published standard.

I can't give you a reliable date for that. The dataset covers reports through roughly late 2020, and the last confirmed *Vespa mandarinia* detection in Washington State was in 2021 (a nest found and destroyed in Whatcom County that fall); after that, no further confirmed detections occurred, and the state declared the hornet eradicated in 2024. If by "dead end" you mean the last confirmed sighting that led to no further detections, that would be the 2021 season. But I have no precise date, and this is outside the provided dataset — treat it as background, not a data point.

I can't give a reliable number. Washington's Asian giant hornet response was run by WSDA with support from USDA and local partners, and the field team doing report follow-ups was small — on the order of a handful of people (roughly 2–6 field staff) available for site visits at any one time, scaling up seasonally when detections clustered. This is an empirical judgment, not a published figure; the dataset contains no staffing information.

I can't give a reliable number, and the dataset itself is the better guide here: it contains 4,440 reports total, so the average across the whole reporting period is only a few per day. In a busy late-summer week — when public awareness peaks and hornets are most visible — the state plausibly receives on the order of tens of new reports per week (roughly 20–100), with spikes after any media coverage of a confirmed detection. That is an empirical judgment, not a published figure; the dataset contains no weekly reporting-rate breakdown.

Late summer to early fall — the peak is typically August and September, with reports tapering off by October. That aligns with the hornet's colony cycle: workers are most numerous and most visible to the public in late summer, and new queens emerge in the fall. Spring and early summer reports are comparatively few. This is an empirical judgment based on the hornet's life cycle and typical reporting patterns, not a figure computed from the dataset.

Confidence comes from sustained absence of detections under adequate surveillance, not from a single clean season. Concretely: multiple consecutive years (typically 3+) with zero confirmed *Vespa mandarinia* despite continued trapping and public reporting at normal or higher intensity; no nest found in systematic searches of the previously infested area; and no confirmed positive among the ongoing report stream, including the high-quality photo reports that historically produced positives. The key condition is that surveillance effort must not have dropped — absence of detections only means eradication if searching was still active and sensitive. A single year of no finds, or a quiet year with reduced trapping and public attention, is not sufficient evidence.

New reports first, not older ones. Investigations are prioritized by likelihood of being a genuine *Vespa mandarinia* and by recency — a fresh report with a clear photo or a description matching the hornet (large orange-and-black head, unusually large size) near the known detection area gets followed up within a day or two, because a live hornet or active nest is time-sensitive and can still be located and destroyed.

Older reports are generally lower priority: the insect is long gone, the trail is cold, and the site visit is unlikely to find anything. Backlogged older reports tend to be worked only if resources allow, or left unprocessed. The exception is a cluster of older reports in one location, which can still be worth a site search for a nest.
